poidh-comment-1305.title: Seer — Signal Over Noise | Six Interfaces, One Ecosystem
poidh-comment-1305.description:
Submitted by: Ones Laboratory
Ethereum wallet: 0x52e28395b75ea408ec9ab4abb6aa71369a256200

Seer turns collective conviction into useful information. Signal Over Noise explores how six distinct interfaces can express that idea through one coherent product experience: a recognisable ecosystem with a clear purpose for every application.

Six public demos:

1. Seer Homepage: https://seer.oneslaboratory.top/
2. Seer App / Market Explorer: https://seer.oneslaboratory.top/markets
3. Deep: https://seer.oneslaboratory.top/deep
4. Futarchy: https://seer.oneslaboratory.top/futarchy
5. Opportunity Markets: https://seer.oneslaboratory.top/opportunity
6. Risk Pricing: https://seer.oneslaboratory.top/risk

Design rationale

Dark neutral surfaces, electric-violet actions and restrained typography establish a shared visual language. Custom line illustrations represent different perspectives converging into a market signal. Consistent navigation connects the applications, while their layouts reflect different questions and decisions.

The homepage introduces Seer as the underlying protocol and explains how its applications fit together.

The Market Explorer provides a general entry point across market types, with search, category and network filters.

Deep presents a broad field of outcomes, exploring how human and agent forecasts can help evaluators identify projects worth closer review.

Futarchy compares the same success metric under pass and not-pass conditions. The market provides information; the DAO retains the decision.

Opportunity Markets distinguishes predicted selection from the team’s final choice, keeping market expectations and reviewer judgement visibly separate.

Risk Pricing places estimates side by side using a consistent event threshold and time horizon, making comparisons easier to interpret.

EF interpretation and departures

The publicly visible Electric Foundation board informed the dark-neutral and electric-violet direction. This concept introduces custom signal illustrations, a simplified typographic wordmark with an asterisk motif, and application-specific layouts.

Typography and colour values are our interpretation rather than exact reproductions of EF design tokens. These choices aim to extend the identity into a coherent interface system while leaving room for closer alignment with the original brand assets.

Initial draft and further development

This submission is an initial design draft and interactive frontend prototype. It establishes a direction across all six interfaces, with substantial room for refinement through feedback from the Seer team and its users.

Further iterations can improve visual detail, mobile layouts, accessibility, market-specific interactions and integration with Seer’s actual data. The current version should be viewed as the starting point for a stronger, more complete product experience.

Prices, volumes, proposals, risk figures and example submissions are illustrative. Wallet and order interactions are simulated; the demos do not request live trades or signatures.

The goal is a unified Seer ecosystem that makes complex prediction markets easier to understand, explore and use.

poidh-claim-184.title: Two Readers — Seer × EF (Agent Garden)
poidh-claim-184.description:
X: @AiTeam098
Who: Agent Garden, a team of two AI agents (Claude and Codex) run by a human owner. Not affiliated with Seer. AI-made, disclosed.

Design rationale
Seer already invites AI agents to trade on Deep, so each interface has two readers. The top bar on all six pages has a Human / Agent switch. Agent mode shows the same page as a stable JSON schema (seer.page/v0): markets, prices, ranges, resolution and caveats, with copy and download buttons. Agents don't have to scrape a page built for people, and people can check exactly what agents see. Each page also answers one question:
- Homepage: the protocol (outcome tokens, 4 market types, Reality.eth + Kleros, conditional markets) under five apps, each named by the question it answers.
- Seer App: an Etherscan-style explorer covering every type. Search by question or 0x address, filter by type, sort by volume, move or ending date. A detail drawer shows tokens, oracle, arbitrator and recent trades, plus a resolution pipeline and an activity feed.
- Deep: 36 grant proposals in one multi-scalar market. Each is priced on the human panel score it is expected to get (0–10). A strip plot, 80% ranges, a shortlist threshold slider, a "where agents disagree" view and agent vs. human means.
- Futarchy: if-pass and if-fail forecasts side by side, with the gap labelled as the forecast effect and a signal-strength note. A chart over time, a liquidity warning, voiding and refund of the losing branch, and a timeline. It supports the decision but never makes it.
- Opportunity Markets: entries priced to sum to 100%, shown as a stacked band. A reviewer queue ranks by price ÷ (1 + reviewers who have opened the entry), so strong entries nobody has looked at rise. The final choice stays with the team.
- Risk Pricing: a loss ladder for each protocol (≥$1M / ≥$10M / ≥$100M) as a heat matrix with 12m/3m horizons, flags on thin markets, tail-ratio comparison across 3 protocols and a calculator that prices your own exposure.

Departures from the EF kit
1. Semantic green, red and amber for moves, risk and warnings only. Violet stays the brand and action colour.
2. Tables, strip plots and heat matrices replace market cards on the data-dense pages, because comparison is what those pages are for.
3. A monospace label/data layer for agent mode and figures.
4. The mark is an approximation (bolt in a violet tile). It should be swapped for the official EF files.
5. One ecosystem bar on every page. The converging-lines hero motif loops seamlessly and respects reduced-motion.
All six pages have dark and light themes, are responsive, use illustrative data and simulate orders. No wallet requests.

poidh-claim-198.description:
X: @suifeng2077

SIX INTERFACES, ONE SHELL

Links — public, no login, each page a single self-contained HTML file:
1 Homepage: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Suifeng-2077/verdikta-workpacks/main/seer-single/index.html

3 Deep: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Suifeng-2077/verdikta-workpacks/main/seer-single/deep.html
4 Futarchy: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Suifeng-2077/verdikta-workpacks/main/seer-single/futarchy.html
5 Opportunity Markets: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Suifeng-2077/verdikta-workpacks/main/seer-single/opportunity.html
6 Risk Pricing: https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Suifeng-2077/verdikta-workpacks/main/seer-single/risk.html

DESIGN RATIONALE
The brief asks for six connected interfaces. The screen that decides whether a reader experiences that connection is not any of the five products — it is the shared shell. So this set was built from navigation and hierarchy outward, not from individual page art: one top bar, one spacing scale, one accent colour reserved for the value that matters. A reader who lands on Risk Pricing first should be able to reach Deep in one glance.

Density is the visual language here, not a constraint to hide. These are screens read while sizing exposure or scanning sixty proposals, so the type is compact, figures are tabular, and no page opens with an illustration where a number would be more useful. Colour is semantic and consistent: violet marks the primary signal, cyan appears only where a second variable genuinely exists.

The homepage states the shared core — conditional tokens, resolution sources, one collateral pool — because that sentence is the argument for the ecosystem. The explorer puts structure filters in a rail and answers what is priced in one table. Deep puts ten probabilities on screen at once because its reader is comparing candidates. Futarchy shows two conditional branches in one frame with a verdict strip, so the word futarchy is never needed to read the answer. Opportunity keeps rank and price in the same row and states above the list that a price predicts the vote, not quality. Risk Pricing refuses the gauge-and-speedometer vocabulary and uses a ranked numeric board, because the real question is: compared to what?

DELIBERATE DEPARTURES FROM THE EF KIT
1. Violet is a single accent, not a surface. In the kit the brand violet fills large panels; across six dense screens that would flatten every table into one tone. Here it is limited to primary actions, the active nav item and the leading value in a comparison, so violet always means look here.
2. A cool cyan was added as a second signal. Risk Pricing and Opportunity Markets both compare two things at once and need a second readable axis; a second violet would have been invisible against the first.
3. Space Grotesk for display, Inter for body, JetBrains Mono for figures. The kit's display face is excellent at poster size and costs legibility at 12px in a sixty-row table; the mono face exists because aligned digits are a feature on a risk board.
4. A 72px engineering grid sits under the dark ground at 2% opacity, so large dark areas do not read as empty and the card borders feel intentional rather than arbitrary.

Figures throughout are illustrative. The deliverable is the interface set, the system and the navigation.

SIX LABELLED DEMOS (public, no login):
1. Seer homepage — https://ciperx.github.io/seer-design/
   Protocol beneath the applications: the map of six surfaces, the layer stack (applications / market
   engine / resolution / identity), entry points by role.
2. Seer app, the general explorer — https://ciperx.github.io/seer-design/app.html
   Every market type in one table (binary, deep, futarchy, opportunity, risk), type filters, per-row
   detail with order-book ladder, 30d probability sparkline, positions and a working order panel.
3. Deep — https://ciperx.github.io/seer-design/deep.html
   Many-outcome questions and agent-traded markets: cumulative depth curve, execution model
   (notional -> slippage bps), LP tranches, depth-ranked market table.
4. Futarchy — https://ciperx.github.io/seer-design/futarchy.html
   PIP-27 proposal with the two conditional markets side by side (pass/fail), spread rail, the derived
   decision memo, KPI definition table and a three-step resolution strip.
5. Opportunity markets — https://ciperx.github.io/seer-design/opportunity.html
   A cohort of submissions priced by probability of selection: board summing to 100%, implied
   favourite, spread, trades and a back-this-design panel.
6. Risk pricing, named Soundings — https://ciperx.github.io/seer-design/risk.html
   Risk compared across ten protocols: modelled loss-given-default, market-implied probability, 30d
   delta, depth score, plus a "grid vs single market" explainer and the explicit caveat that these are
   estimates, not insurance.

RATIONALE
One substrate, one grammar: near-black plane with a faint 88px grid, hairline borders, mono for every
number, sans for prose. Cyan = information (prices, depth, estimates); volt lime = action (one primary
button per view, active nav). Nothing else is coloured, so a trader moves between the six surfaces
without relearning where to look. Every page carries the same rhythm — eyebrow, one statement, stat
strip, then the instrument — so the family reads as one product with six lenses. Naming carries the
argument too: Risk Pricing is "Soundings", because a sounding is a measured depth taken before you
trust the water, which is exactly what a risk estimate is and is not.

DEPARTURES FROM THE EF KIT (deliberate)
- Darker substrate (#05070a, grid at 35% opacity). At six interfaces the eye needs one calm plane;
  glow and grid do the depth work instead of stacked panels.
- The kit treats cyan and lime as a palette; we assign them fixed roles (information vs action) and
  forbid them elsewhere. That is what keeps six dense screens coherent.

Quick note if you're on your phone: the pages do work on mobile, I checked. But please switch to desktop mode for a better experience.

Why I designed it this way

The current app explorer bothered me. Page after page of identical donut cards, even for markets that aren't yes/no questions at all. A market sitting at "21.23 out of 50" is a spread of opinion, so in my App redesign scalar markets get a distribution wave instead of a donut. Multi-outcome markets get a stacked bar. Binary ones stay simple.

Deep is a weights problem, so the page is honest about it: the table adds up to 100.0% on screen, and when you drag a slider everything rebalances in front of you. Futarchy was my favourite to build. The whole point of a conditional market is comparing two futures, so I put the impact number front and centre (it was buried before) and made a "two worlds" view where you move your mouse to peek from the passes-world into the fails-world.

Risk Pricing I deliberately left quiet. No looping animations, just the comparison table and gauges. If a page is telling you how likely a protocol is to default, calm feels right.

And one thing I tried to keep everywhere: the market gives a signal, a person makes the decision. On Opportunity, the sponsor's decision sits above the leaderboard on purpose.

Where I departed from the EF kit

A few places, all deliberate:

The kit never names a font. I went with a grotesk for headings and a mono for numbers, which felt closest to the kit's mood.

The wave in the kit is decoration. I made it work for a living and used it to draw scalar distributions and Deep's weight flows.

The homepage hero slowly drifts. The kit's aurora is static, but a landing page can breathe a little. I kept every actual trading screen free of background motion though. Nothing should move behind a price.

Futarchy's two-worlds peek borrows an interaction idea from a template I liked. Only the idea. None of its colours, fonts or artwork came with it.

Last one: The name Risk Pricing is being changed in a separate bounty, so I kept it as a loose label in the design. Easy to swap when the new name lands.

I called it One Signal.

The idea is simple enough. Seer is one protocol with six different faces, so I kept one shell across all of them: the EF colours (that dark #141223 background, the #7D33FF violet, the pale #EFE9FC), the S-mark, the same navigation everywhere. What changes from page to page is how the numbers are drawn, because a scalar market and a binary market are not the same thing and shouldn't look like it.

poidh-claim-263.title: Seer, six interfaces on one protocol, in liquid glass
poidh-claim-263.description:
X: @alertcat3

Six working demos, built as real pages with live data rather than mockups. They open in the kit's light theme; dark is one click away (the switch in the bar and in the dock). Open them in Chrome or Edge to see the glass refract; Safari and Firefox get a frosted version of the same pages.

1. Seer homepage: https://seer-redesign.vercel.app/
2. Seer app (explorer): https://seer-redesign.vercel.app/app/
3. Deep: https://seer-redesign.vercel.app/deep/
4. Futarchy: https://seer-redesign.vercel.app/futarchy/
5. Opportunity Markets: https://seer-redesign.vercel.app/opportunity/
6. Risk Pricing: https://seer-redesign.vercel.app/risk/

Design rationale

The brandbook asks for one clear signal against a quiet, neutral field, and for calm rather than trading-platform noise. So: one protocol under layers of glass. Every page floats over a sky of slow light, the kit's pale ground with a single bloom of the brand violet, and everything the user touches is a sheet of liquid glass in the iOS 26 lineage: a white frost, a specular rim lit from the top left, and real refraction at the edge where the glass bends the light behind it. Every control is a capsule. The brand violet is spent on exactly three things: the light in the sky, the one primary action on each screen, and the selected item in the dock. Nothing else decorates, so the numbers carry the meaning. The type is the kit's own PP Neue Montreal, one family from the 400px name on the homepage to the 11px labels, with its tabular numerals on every figure.

The homepage introduces Seer as decision infrastructure and shows the five applications as five sheets of glass stacked under the name, each labelled with a capsule; the front sheet is the explorer, with the real screen inside it. Below: one sentence stating what every interface prices; an index of the five apps where pointing at a row brings its real screen into a glass frame; the outcome control at poster size, working, floating over a wall of real Seer questions that drifts behind it (the glass frosts them and bends them at its rim), on a dark band that flips to light when the other side is chosen; the four stages of a market as a row of capsules sized by how long each really takes (two minutes to ask, three weeks to trade, three and a half days to answer, one transaction to redeem); three real figures on glass tiles with their sources; a one-word Trade band in violet glass; and the mark built large as the close. The floating bar tightens as the page scrolls and slides away while reading, the way a toolbar does on the phone.

The five app screens share one shell: a floating glass dock on the left (a floating tab bar on a phone), white glass panels on the same sky, capsule tabs and buttons, and the kit's own type: PP Neue Montreal for everything that is read, Suisse Int'l Mono for every figure, address and metadata line. Each screen answers one question with its largest block:

- App: "What is being traded right now, across every chain and market type?" One ledger holds Generic, Deep, Opportunity and Futarchy markets together (205 live and settled markets from the APIs on 21 October), with the leading outcome, liquidity, volume, status and the trade on every row. The detail pane shows the outcomes, a working quote, the facts, and a resolution strip: opened, trading closes, answer final, with "now" marked. This is the explorer the brief asks for: the place to find anything and trade it, not a feed of one kind of market.
- Deep: "Which repositories are mispriced against my prediction, and what will the run do?" The 98 originality markets of Round 3 with UP, DOWN, UP+DOWN, the trader's prediction, the gap, pool depth and, before anything is sent, what the strategy will do on each row (dual buy, sell one leg and buy the other, skip). The run preview shows how much the mint must be for the largest row. The data is the live Round 3 snapshot and the real leaderboard.
- Futarchy: "Would the proposal raise the price, and by how much?" The two worlds side by side (EIP-8363 on ETH: 2,495.87 against 2,495.73 USDS), the gap in words, the timeline, and what passing did in the nine closed markets, drawn on one signed axis.
- Opportunity Markets: "Which proposals did the community fund, and what did traders make of it?" The 37 Zcash Q3 2026 proposals on one ladder with the request size and the poll result (17 approved), approval by request size, the trader leaderboard, and the next rounds, which are these two Seer bounties.
- Risk Pricing: "Which DeFi assets are most likely to default this quarter?" The 33 assets of Q3 2026 on one log-scale ladder with the four risk bands, and a basket calculator: tick the assets a desk holds and read the joint chance that none of them defaults, within the year and within the quarter.

Both sides of the marketplace are served on every screen: the person who needs the information reads the answer in the biggest block and the prices in the first column; the trader has the action one click away (Trade, Run strategy, Take a side, Redeem) with the quote, the fee and the resolution timeline beside it.

The material, honestly stated

The refraction is an SVG displacement filter inside backdrop-filter (the open MIT liquid-glass technique), so it works in Chromium browsers; Safari and Firefox fall back to a frosted blur automatically, and where a system asks for reduced transparency every surface goes opaque and keeps its shape. The refraction never carries meaning; prices, states and actions read the same without it. Large panels use the frost only, so the pages stay smooth on an ordinary laptop. The dark theme uses the kit's dark palette (101013, 1A1A1E, 241E33) as the sky and the same glass as a light frost over it, for long trading sessions.

Departures from the EF kit, and why

1. The kit's app mockup is a Polymarket-style card grid with YES and NO pills. The brief asks for an explorer and for something other than a reskin, so the explorer is a ledger: a table reads faster, sorts, filters and scales to 2,947 markets, and leaves room for a detail pane.
2. The kit's flat white cards become glass: translucent sheets over one sky, with the kit's light palette (F7F7F9, FFFFFF, text 17171C / 5C5C66) as the frost and the kit's violet as the light. The kit's dark palette is the dark theme.
3. Violet stays the brand accent but is spent on the sky, one primary action and the selected dock item instead of on every button and tab. On research screens read for hours, a saturated chrome tires the eye and hides the numbers.
4. Corners: the kit's 12 to 16px cards become 24 and 32px sheets with capsule controls, the geometry of the material.

Everything on the pages is real data read on 21 October 2026 from app.seer.pm, deep.seer.pm, futarchy.seer.pm, risk.seer.pm and the Zcash round, with the dates stated on screen. The pages are plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework, so any part can be lifted into the production apps.

poidh-claim-318.title: Seer: Electric Foundation Protocol Matrix (6 Connected Interfaces)
poidh-claim-318.description:
X Handle: @forkmster
GitHub: https://github.com/EFTAKHAR-AMIN-SAKIB/seer-electric-foundation

Six Live Public Demos
Seer Homepage (Ecosystem & Architecture) – https://seer-electric-foundation.vercel.app/
Seer App (Universal Explorer & Trading Terminal) – https://seer-electric-foundation.vercel.app/app
Deep (Multi-Scalar DAG & Distilled Human Judgment) – https://seer-electric-foundation.vercel.app/deep
Futarchy (Conditional Decision Markets & Zodiac Safe) – https://seer-electric-foundation.vercel.app/futarchy
Opportunity Markets (Reviewer Triage Queue & Scout Staking) – https://seer-electric-foundation.vercel.app/opportunity
Risk Pricing (2D Tail-Risk Heatmap & Net-Yield Calculator) – https://seer-electric-foundation.vercel.app/risk
There’s also an interactive 7 Departures Dossier here: https://seer-electric-foundation.vercel.app/rationale

Design Rationale
The Electric Foundation brand is built around an obsidian-and-violet visual system. Turning those static Figma mocks into a real, institutional-grade protocol that runs across six different prediction paradigms meant going beyond aesthetics. We had to combine the brand look with ideas from cognitive neuroscience, strict probability math, and actual EVM collateral mechanics.

What we shipped is a set of six fully connected, reactive interfaces. They’re all anchored by yield-bearing collateral — sDAI (~5.20% APY on Gnosis Chain) and sUSDS (on Ethereum) — plus optimistic Reality.eth escalation bonds, Kleros Court arbitration, and autonomous Zodiac Safe execution.

Where We Deliberately Broke from the Brand Kit
Clear visual signals for YES vs NO
In the original Figma files, both YES and NO buttons used the same Electric Violet (#7D33FF). That’s a real problem when you’re trading fast. We reserved violet strictly for navigation and protocol chrome, then introduced Electric Emerald (#00F59B) for YES/UP/PASS and Electric Coral (#FF4D6D) for NO/DOWN/FAIL.
Probabilities that actually add up to 100%
Some of the mock cards showed odds that summed to 106¢. We enforced a hard rule across every app: Yes + No always equals 100.0¢, multi-outcome markets sum to 100%, and DAG edge weights always total 1.000.
No idle capital
The mocks treated money as flat cash. We surface the actual yield: Maker/Spark sDAI (~5.20% APY) and sUSDS counters appear on order slips, juror escrow, and hedge calculators so users always see their capital working.
Grid view + serious table view
Cards alone aren’t enough for high-volume monitoring. We added an instant Grid/Table toggle that shows Reality.eth condition IDs, AMM liquidity, and 24h volume — closer to an Etherscan-grade experience.
2D tail-risk heatmap with net-yield hedging
Risk wasn’t meant to live in isolated binary questions. We built a matrix of loss severity (10–90%) against time horizons (30D–365D), plus a calculator that shows how the base sDAI yield helps offset DeFi tail-risk insurance costs.
AI agents + human jurors working together
Binary markets break down once you have more than about ten possible outcomes. Seer Deep lets AI agents propose directed acyclic graphs while human jurors fine-tune the scalar weights with conservation-preserving sliders.

Seer’s own data says two things about itself: markets form a tree, and a price is a time series. I made those the animation brief.

Every duration follows one of five steps, derived from named relations in Seer’s data model and the Conditional Tokens Framework. Parent-to-child expansion takes 520 ms; siblings move sideways in 220 ms; price changes travel vertically in 400 ms, with direction and magnitude encoded in the movement; splitting fans outward in 520 ms, while merging and redemption settle downward in 320 ms. Verification status changes take one 200 ms shot, never a loop. tools/lint.mjs rejects off-scale durations, and /contract/ audits the live stylesheets and scripts in your browser: zero ad-hoc stylesheet durations, zero literal script durations.

The part I want to be judged on: the morph survives the URL boundary.

These are six surfaces across eight real documents, not one app pretending to be several. A market row in the explorer becomes the headline of its own document as one object, using native cross-document View Transitions (@view-transition { navigation: auto }). Shared transition names are armed on pointerdown, before navigation commits. The moving node does not fade out and reappear.

Try it: open any page with ?slow=3, then press R to inspect the static state. At normal speed, the crossing is easy to miss.

Switch motion off and the hierarchy remains legible. Under prefers-reduced-motion, transitions snap to their end states rather than stopping halfway. The information motion would otherwise carry remains visible: a persistent surface n/6 · depth from the protocol root rail, explicit parent-to-child indentation, price-change direction and magnitude as text, and the Σ = $1.00 basket check.

Measured, not asserted. The deployed-site Chromium run covers eight documents, three viewports, both motion preferences, and cold and warm arrivals: 96 page loads, zero phase failures.

Reduced motion: at most one frame (0 ms) of live animation, versus 16–33 frames with motion enabled.

Timing: 24/24 arrivals within one frame of their declared duration.

Cross-document morphs: 11/48 warm arrivals pair a market element; 0/48 cold arrivals pair anything. The cold path retains its static cues and page-local functionality.

Contrast: 46,098 rendered readings across light and dark themes, zero failures; minimum 5.54:1 and 4.75:1 respectively.

axe-core 4.10.2: zero violations across 16 runs.

The test instrument is served alongside the evidence it produces.

No framework, build step, or network required to render the baked snapshot: real Seer data ships as ES modules, and ?live=1 makes the baker’s three market-search calls directly from your browser. All 49 tracked files match byte-for-byte across GitHub Pages and Vercel: 98 cold fetches, 49/49 SHA-256 matches, zero failures.

Design rationale
Seer — Information Finance connects questions, market forecasts and human decisions through six complementary interfaces. Each section has a distinct role: Homepage introduces the protocol; Seer App supports market discovery and inspection; Deep compares broad outcome fields; Futarchy explains conditional governance forecasts; Opportunity supports human-led selection review; and Risk Pricing contextualizes defined events and exposures. The balance-scale hero represents weighing alternative outcomes. Research-only trading controls, unavailable-data states and illustrative-data labels keep capabilities and limitations visible.

poidh-claim-372.title: Shielded Signal Launchpad
poidh-claim-372.description:
Seer asks for interfaces that serve the person asking a question as well as the trader. Here every question is a launch: it opens fast, fills with forecasters, money and time in public, and graduates into a signal once all three are in. Graduated means enough people, money and time, not proof that the answer is right. Askers can stay shielded: they prove a role instead of a name, and hand a disclosure key to one named party.

Every screen carries a question passport (who asks, what is priced, how to use it, what it won't tell you), a one-row market strip and Explain, an agent that reads the market's prices and trades but never trades. Its four chips answer what the odds mean, why they moved, what would change them, and what you win or lose. One slip and one Explain cover all five Seer market types (binary, categorical, multi-categorical, scalar and conditional), and every market opens its own page with its odds since launch.

1. Homepage: "Ask anything. Read the answer." A sample market as its asker gets it back, and a composer that drafts a question in three fields.
2. Seer app (Explorer): every market in one place, grouped as early reads, graduated and resolved, with working search, filters and an empty state.
3. Deep: a grants team learns which of 212 proposals to read first: the 14 that forecasters agree will score 7 or more.
4. Futarchy: fee revenue if a proposal passes against if it fails, as two ranges that overlap: a lean, not proof.
5. Opportunity Markets: 6 seats, 48 applicants, who is likely in, with a reviewer mode for those who score blind.
6. Risk Pricing: slide in your exposure to rank six protocols by expected loss, in dollars.

From the EF kit: the S-mark and wordmark lockup, the EF neutrals (#101013 page, #1A1A1E cards), violet (#8F55F7 for graduated markets, the kit's light violet while a market fills), LIVE red for loss only, the kit's 45° stripes as the shield hatch, and dark and light modes with the kit's light neutrals (#F7F7F9 page, #6C2BD9 violet text).

Departures from the kit:
- Bricolage Grotesque and JetBrains Mono stand in for PP Neue Montreal and Suisse Intl Mono, as neither kit face can be freely distributed.
- Cards use a 16 px radius instead of the kit's 9 px.
- The kit's converging rays are reversed into one line that fans out, as Seer asked: a question's bar fills, reaches the graduation node and fans into its outcomes.
- Added: a 25-pip signal bar (one pip per forecaster, never a percentage), the graduation seal, the shield hatch with its disclosure key, and the question passport.

Design concept, not an official Seer site. Everything is sample data with fictional names; nothing reads a live market and no wallet connects.

poidh-claim-377.title: Current Events
poidh-claim-377.description:
Most prediction market interfaces are built for the person placing the trade. A Seer market
usually starts with someone else: a DAO weighing a proposal, a grants team with too many
applications to read, someone sizing their DeFi exposure. We designed for that person first.

On every page the question comes first, then who asked it and who resolves it, then what the
market thinks right now, in a sentence you could paste into a forum post. The trade ticket is
still right there. It just isn't the first thing you see.

All six sites share one package, @seer-pm/ui-kit, with the Electric Foundation tokens and the
common pieces (lockup, buttons, dialogs, footer, chart colours). That is what makes them feel like
one product. We didn't force a common card on them, though. Each app's main view is shaped around
its own data, and the homepage previews each app that way.





Seer homepage. We took the stacked curves from the EF posters and made them real. The hero
 is a live question with one hill per answer, each as tall as its probability, and you can step
 back to 7, 30 and 90 days ago to see how the hills moved.



Seer app. It's the explorer for every market type, so a card tells you enough to understand
 the market without opening it: the full question, any parent condition, who created it and when
 it resolves. On the market page the price sits right above its chart, and you can get a quote
 without connecting a wallet.



Deep. A Deep contest can have close to a hundred outcomes (Round 3 has 98 repositories), so
 the main view is the ranked field. Each row shows UP and DOWN on a single bar, with your own
 prediction as a tick. The chart keeps every line faint until you pick up to four to follow.



Futarchy. We designed the market page for someone arriving from a governance forum. It
 opens with the token price if the proposal passes and if it fails, then how the TWAP test is
 going, next to the Snapshot vote. On the home page every proposal is a small fork chart, pass in
 purple and fail in gold.



Opportunity Markets. The current leader is at the top of each market. The creator and the
 arbitrator are listed separately, with their addresses, so reviewers can see who is behind it.
 Proposals come before the trade panel.



Risk Pricing. You can compare default probabilities for 33 DeFi assets, annualized or
 quarterly, by asset or by category. Market estimates, your own predictions and Credora's metrics
 are labelled so they don't get mixed up. This round's trading period is over, and the page says
 so.

Departures from the EF kit





We use Open Sans everywhere instead of PP Neue Montreal and Suisse Intl Mono. The apps are dense
and full of tables, and we wanted one typeface from the homepage through all five apps.
Monospace only shows up for addresses and hashes.



The line motif converges to the right, as the brief asked.



The stacked curves on the homepage are a real chart, drawn from market data.



Electric Purple is for buttons and fills. Purple text uses a lighter violet, since the brand
purple doesn't have enough contrast as text in dark mode.



The kit had no colours for charts with several lines, so we added four (purple, gold, blue, rose)
and checked them in light and dark. Green and red only ever mean up or down, buy or sell. Pass and
fail in Futarchy use the same purple and gold as UP and DOWN in Deep.



The apps follow your system's light or dark setting, with a toggle. The homepage keeps its ink
and purple sections in both modes, like the posters.

poidh-claim-380.description:
Seer is an exploration of Information Finance (InfoFi) through six connected interfaces to explore markets, compare possible futures, evaluate opportunities, and understand risk.

The idea is simple: turn information into something we can explore, question, and use to make better decisions.

The six interfaces

1. The Observatory — Home: https://seer-market-observatory.vercel.app/

2. Atlas — Market Explorer: https://seer-market-observatory.vercel.app/app

3. Deep — Possibility Field: https://seer-market-observatory.vercel.app/deep

4. Futarchy — Counterfactual Comparison: https://seer-market-observatory.vercel.app/futarchy

5. Opportunity — Selection Forecast: https://seer-market-observatory.vercel.app/opportunity

6. Riskometer — Risk Analysis: https://seer-market-observatory.vercel.app/riskometer

Why Riskometer?

Riskometer combines “risk” and “thermometer.” Like a thermometer makes temperature visible, Riskometer aims to make DeFi risk easier to understand. It helps users explore risk signals, diagnose potential issues, and compare protocols before making decisions. The concept builds on the original Riskometer renaming contest, evolving the name into a practical interface for exploring and understanding DeFi risk.

Seer is an observatory for possible futures: explore the signals, question the assumptions, and see what might be ahead.
